records.statement: Weekly resistance-training set volume is positively associated with strength and hypertrophy gains at group level, with diminishing returns; frequency has a clearer independent relationship with strength than with hypertrophy.
records.applies_to: Predominantly young healthy adults represented in resistance-training dose studies.
allowed_language: More weekly sets can produce additional adaptation, but returns diminish.
Frequency can help distribute volume and practice lifts.
disallowed_language: More sets are always better.
The model identifies your optimal weekly set count.
records.limitations: Cross-study meta-regression cannot define an individual optimum; direct and indirect set counting, adherence and recovery capacity remain important uncertainties.

records.statement: Resistance training reliably improves muscle mass and strength, but evidence is insufficient to declare many isolated prescription variables universally superior.
allowed_language: The whole program matters more than one isolated variable.
Several training configurations can work.
disallowed_language: Research proves one universally best split, tempo or rest interval.
A single variable determines the result.
records.limitations: Umbrella reviews depend on the quality and overlap of prior reviews and do not replace goal-specific or population-specific evidence.

records.statement: When total training volume is equated, periodized resistance training may improve 1RM strength more than non-periodized training, particularly in trained participants, without a clear hypertrophy advantage.
records.applies_to: Healthy adults in volume-equated resistance-training studies, with the clearest strength evidence in trained participants.
allowed_language: Planned variation can be useful for strength development.
Periodization organizes training; it is not a separate growth stimulus.
disallowed_language: Undulating periodization is best for everyone.
Periodization automatically produces more hypertrophy.
records.limitations: Evidence beyond linear versus undulating models was sparse, and subgroup estimates in trained people were imprecise.

records.statement: Both short and longer inter-set rests can support hypertrophy; rests longer than 60 seconds may have a small advantage, while evidence does not show meaningful additional hypertrophy beyond roughly 90 seconds.
records.applies_to: Healthy adults performing conventional resistance training for hypertrophy.
allowed_language: Rest long enough to preserve the intended work quality.
Rest interval is a program variable, not a universal timer.
disallowed_language: Exactly 90 seconds is optimal for every set.
Short rests prevent muscle growth.
records.limitations: The evidence included only nine heterogeneous studies and does not resolve goal, exercise, load or time-efficiency tradeoffs.

records.statement: Hypertrophy outcomes were broadly similar across repetition durations of approximately 0.5 to 8 seconds in a small evidence base; deliberately very slow repetitions are not established as superior.
records.applies_to: Healthy people performing dynamic resistance training, usually with sets taken to failure.
allowed_language: A range of controlled repetition speeds can build muscle.
Tempo can serve technique and task intent.
disallowed_language: One tempo code maximizes hypertrophy.
Slower repetitions always create more growth.
records.limitations: Only eight studies qualified and findings may not transfer to power training, submaximal sets or every exercise.

records.statement: Within-set velocity loss reflects accumulating repetitions and fatigue, but different thresholds involve tradeoffs among hypertrophy, strength efficiency, jump, sprint and velocity outcomes.
records.applies_to: Mostly trained adults using validated velocity-measurement devices during resistance training.
allowed_language: Velocity loss can help standardize set termination when a device is available.
The threshold should match the training outcome and exercise.
disallowed_language: A single velocity-loss threshold is best for all goals.
Phone-estimated velocity proves fatigue or readiness.
records.limitations: Threshold effects vary by exercise, load and training history; device validity and protocol consistency are prerequisites.

records.statement: RPE-, RIR- and velocity-based autoregulation are viable load-management approaches, but current evidence does not establish a consistent overall advantage over well-designed percentage-based training.
records.applies_to: Resistance-trained people in short load- and volume-autoregulation studies.
allowed_language: Autoregulation is one way to adjust training to observed session performance.
Fixed and autoregulated methods can both work.
disallowed_language: Autoregulation is proven superior for every trainee.
An AI estimate can replace measured velocity or experienced RIR judgment.
records.limitations: Trials were few, short and small; hypertrophy evidence was particularly limited and app-only implementation was not tested.

records.statement: Polarized, pyramidal and other endurance intensity distributions can all improve performance; current comparative evidence does not support one universally superior model, and training level may modify response.
records.applies_to: Recreational to highly trained endurance athletes.
allowed_language: Most endurance programs distribute work across more than one intensity domain.
Training level and the outcome measured affect how intensity-distribution evidence is interpreted.
disallowed_language: Polarized training is scientifically best for everyone.
An elite intensity distribution should be copied by a beginner.
records.limitations: Zone definitions and quantification methods varied, women were underrepresented, and direct comparisons were limited.

records.statement: Reducing training volume while maintaining some intensity before competition can improve endurance time-trial performance at group level.
records.applies_to: Endurance athletes approaching a planned performance test or competition.
allowed_language: A taper reduces accumulated training demand before an event.
Taper design should preserve event-specific exposure while reducing volume.
disallowed_language: A fixed percentage reduction guarantees peak performance.
Every recreational exerciser needs a competition taper.
records.limitations: Only 14 heterogeneous studies were included and subgroup prescriptions are not precise individual rules.

records.statement: Training monitoring should distinguish external work performed from the person's internal response and should use consistent, interpretable measures rather than a single universal load score.
records.applies_to: Athletes and recreational users whose training sessions are monitored over time.
allowed_language: Duration and work describe external exposure; RPE describes part of the internal response.
Trends are more interpretable when collection is consistent.
disallowed_language: One load number measures total physiological stress.
A workload ratio predicts injury for this person.
records.limitations: Consensus frameworks do not validate SportRX metrics, thresholds or causal predictions.

records.statement: Recovery is multidimensional and varies within and between people; no single self-report or physiological marker provides a complete recovery state.
records.applies_to: Athletes and recreational exercisers considering fatigue and recovery between sessions.
allowed_language: Recovery should be interpreted from multiple observations over time.
Training stress and non-training demands can both affect the current picture.
disallowed_language: One score proves full recovery.
A low RPE means the athlete is recovered.
records.limitations: The consensus is a conceptual framework and does not validate a SportRX recovery score or a personal decision threshold.

records.statement: Nonfunctional overreaching and overtraining syndrome cannot be diagnosed from one symptom, biomarker, RPE trend or performance decline; overtraining syndrome requires clinical exclusion of other causes.
records.applies_to: Research and professional evaluation of athletes with persistent performance decline and fatigue.
allowed_language: Persistent unexplained deterioration needs professional assessment.
SportRX monitoring cannot diagnose overtraining syndrome.
disallowed_language: Your data show overtraining syndrome.
A fatigue score medically clears continued training.
records.limitations: The statement predates newer monitoring technologies, but the absence of a single accepted diagnostic marker remains a critical boundary.

records.statement: Repeated stretching can increase joint range of motion in healthy adults, but flexibility improvement does not by itself demonstrate injury prevention, pain treatment or better sport performance.
records.applies_to: Healthy adults using stretching to improve range of motion.
allowed_language: Static stretching is one effective way to improve flexibility.
Baseline flexibility and the joint tested affect interpretation.
disallowed_language: More flexibility always reduces injury risk.
Stretching treats pain or guarantees better performance.
records.limitations: Studies and tests were heterogeneous and primarily measured range of motion, not clinical or sport outcomes.

records.statement: Meta-regression suggests static-stretching flexibility gains plateau at a modest group-level volume, but those estimates are not validated personal dose ceilings.
records.applies_to: Adults performing acute or chronic static stretching for flexibility.
allowed_language: Very large stretching volumes may not add further flexibility benefit.
Use measured range of motion and tolerance to review progress.
disallowed_language: Ten minutes per week is the exact dose for every joint.
Stretch to pain to maximize results.
records.limitations: Dose-response estimates combine different joints, tests and populations and do not define safe individual intensity.

records.statement: Lower-body plyometric training can improve jumping, sprint performance and lower-body strength in healthy active adults and athletes over several weeks.
records.applies_to: Healthy recreationally active adults and athletes with appropriate movement preparation.
allowed_language: Plyometric training is a targeted option for jump and sprint qualities.
Progression should consider landing skill, exposure and task demands.
disallowed_language: Plyometrics are appropriate for every beginner.
The review defines a safe personal jump dose.
records.limitations: Interventions and participant training levels varied, and the review did not validate readiness screening or exercise progression rules.

records.statement: Both interval and continuous endurance training can improve cardiorespiratory fitness; interval training can offer additional average gains in some populations but is not a universal default.
records.applies_to: Healthy young-to-older adults after appropriate screening and progression review.
allowed_language: Intervals and continuous work are both valid aerobic tools.
Protocol, training history and tolerance matter.
disallowed_language: HIIT is always superior and time-efficient for everyone.
A meta-analysis proves this interval dose is safe for you.
records.limitations: Reviews included heterogeneous protocols and short interventions; comparative fitness effects do not establish personal safety or adherence.

records.statement: Reduced training frequency or volume may maintain some endurance and strength adaptations for limited periods when intensity is preserved, but maintenance and improvement are different objectives.
records.applies_to: Previously trained adults facing temporary time constraints.
allowed_language: A maintenance block can intentionally use less volume than a development block.
Prior training status matters when reducing dose.
disallowed_language: One weekly set maintains everyone indefinitely.
A maintenance dose will continue producing improvement.
records.limitations: The source is a narrative review and direct evidence is limited for athletes, older adults, women and long durations.
